title: Lymph Biochemistry: Chylomicrons and Lymph Protein
subject: Immune and Lymphatic System (IMMU)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows two things that lymph carries. Intestinal lymph carries dietary fat, which enterocytes package as chylomicrons that travel through lacteals and the thoracic duct into the blood without first passing through the liver. In the blood, lipoprotein lipase strips their triglyceride for muscle and adipose tissue, and the liver clears the remnant. Lymph also returns plasma protein that has leaked out of capillaries, and how much it carries depends on how leaky the local endothelium is. Board questions ask you to trace a chylomicron, name the protein acting at each step, predict what happens when one is missing, and explain why liver and gut lymph are rich in protein while muscle lymph is not.
prerequisites: Luminal fat digestion by pancreatic lipase and micelle formation by bile salts (GI-6, GI-7)
General structure of lipoproteins: a neutral lipid core inside a phospholipid, free cholesterol, and apolipoprotein shell
Protein synthesis on the rough ER, ER to Golgi transport, and proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins
Lymph formation and the course of the thoracic duct (IM-4, IM-9)

The chylomicron pathway is the exogenous half of lipoprotein metabolism, and its enzyme and apolipoprotein defects are the type I and type III dyslipidemias.

sections.title: Chylomicron assembly in the enterocyte and the lymphatic route to the blood

blocks.text: Triglyceride cannot cross a membrane intact. In the gut lumen, pancreatic lipase cuts it into 2-monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids, and bile salt micelles carry these to the brush border, where they enter the enterocyte. Inside the cell, fatty acid binding proteins carry long chain fatty acids to the smooth ER. There, acyl-CoA synthetase activates each fatty acid to fatty acyl-CoA, and two acyltransferases (monoacylglycerol acyltransferase, then diacylglycerol acyltransferase) rebuild triglyceride. Absorbed cholesterol is esterified by acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT), and lysophospholipids are reacylated.

Neutral lipid must be wrapped in an amphipathic shell before it can travel in water. The structural protein of that shell is apoB-48. The APOB gene is transcribed in both liver and intestine, but in the intestine the editing enzyme APOBEC-1 deaminates a single cytidine in the mRNA to uridine, changing a glutamine codon (CAA) into a stop codon (UAA). Translation ends about halfway, giving apoB-48, which lacks the carboxy-terminal region that binds the LDL receptor. The liver does not edit the message and makes full-length apoB-100.

Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) works in the ER lumen, loading triglyceride, cholesteryl ester, and phospholipid onto apoB-48 while it is still being translated. Unlipidated apoB misfolds and is degraded by the proteasome, so MTP decides whether any particle forms at all. The nascent particle, which also carries apoA-I and apoA-IV, moves to the Golgi in a specialized prechylomicron transport vesicle (a step that needs the GTPase SAR1B), is glycosylated, and leaves by exocytosis from the basolateral membrane into the lamina propria. A chylomicron is about 85 to 90% triglyceride by mass and roughly 100 to 1,000 nm across.

blocks.title: Chylomicron assembly and transport to the blood
steps: Micelles deliver 2-monoacylglycerol and fatty acids to the enterocyte
Fatty acids activated to acyl-CoA; smooth ER rebuilds triglyceride
MTP loads lipid onto apoB-48 as it is translated
Prechylomicron vesicle carries the particle to the Golgi
Basolateral exocytosis into the lamina propria
Entry into the lacteal, then mesenteric lymph and cisterna chyli
Thoracic duct empties into the left venous angle
blocks.caption: Dietary long chain fat leaves the gut packaged as chylomicrons and reaches the systemic veins through lymph, not the portal vein.

blocks.text: Chylomicrons are too large to pass through the fenestrae and basement membrane of the villus blood capillaries. Lacteals have a discontinuous basement membrane and loose, overlapping endothelial junctions that act as flap valves, so the particles enter lymph instead. They travel through mesenteric lymph vessels and nodes to the cisterna chyli, up the thoracic duct, and into the blood at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. The first capillary beds dietary triglyceride meets are therefore in muscle, heart, and adipose tissue, not the liver.

blocks.title: Two routes for absorbed fat
cols: Long chain fatty acids (more than 12 carbons)
Short and medium chain fatty acids (12 carbons or fewer)
rows: Depends on MTP and lymph flow
blocks.caption: Shorter fatty acids are water soluble enough to diffuse into portal blood, so they are absorbed even when chylomicron formation or lymph flow fails.

blocks.predict: If the thoracic duct were tied off just above the cisterna chyli, what would happen to absorption of a meal containing long chain fat and one containing only medium chain fat?
blocks.explain: Long chain fat would still be packaged into chylomicrons but could not reach the blood by its normal route, so chyle would back up in the intestinal lymphatics and long chain fat absorption would be impaired. Medium chain fatty acids would be absorbed normally because they go straight to portal blood.

sections.title: Chylomicron breakdown: lipoprotein lipase, apoC-II, and apoE

blocks.text: A newly secreted (nascent) chylomicron cannot yet be unloaded. In the plasma it receives apoC-II and apoE from HDL and becomes a mature chylomicron. ApoC-II is the essential activator of lipoprotein lipase (LPL); apoC-III, also acquired from HDL, inhibits LPL and slows clearance.

LPL is made by adipocytes, cardiac and skeletal myocytes, and lactating mammary cells, secreted, and carried to the luminal surface of the neighboring capillary endothelium, where GPIHBP1 and heparan sulfate proteoglycans anchor it. Triglyceride is therefore hydrolyzed inside the capillary. The released fatty acids cross into the adjacent tissue: muscle and heart oxidize them, and adipocytes re-esterify them for storage. Glycerol travels to the liver, which phosphorylates it with glycerol kinase for gluconeogenesis or triglyceride synthesis. Adipocytes have little glycerol kinase, so they make the glycerol 3-phosphate backbone for storage from glucose, which is one reason fat storage depends on insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.

LPL activity is regulated by tissue and by feeding. Insulin increases LPL in adipose tissue after a meal, directing fat to storage. Cardiac LPL has a much lower Km for triglyceride than adipose LPL, so the heart keeps extracting fatty acids even when plasma triglyceride is low during fasting.

blocks.title: Chylomicron breakdown and remnant clearance
steps: HDL transfers apoC-II and apoE to the nascent chylomicron
ApoC-II activates LPL on muscle, heart, and adipose capillaries
LPL hydrolyzes core triglyceride to fatty acids and glycerol
Fatty acids enter tissue; glycerol goes to the liver
Shrinking particle returns apoC-II to HDL
Cholesterol-rich remnant keeps apoB-48 and apoE
ApoE binds hepatic LDL receptor and LRP1; remnant endocytosed
blocks.caption: The particle is emptied of triglyceride in peripheral capillaries, and only the cholesterol-rich remnant reaches the liver.

blocks.text: As the core shrinks, surface phospholipid and apoC-II return to HDL, leaving a smaller, cholesterol-enriched remnant. Because apoB-48 lacks the LDL receptor binding domain, the liver recognizes the remnant only through apoE, which binds the LDL receptor and LDL receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) after the particle is captured on heparan sulfate in the space of Disse; hepatic lipase trims it further. The liver thus receives dietary cholesterol and fat-soluble vitamins (vitamin A is stored in hepatic stellate cells), and the incoming cholesterol suppresses hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Chylomicrons are normally cleared within a few hours of a meal, so plasma after a 12 to 14 hour fast contains essentially none.

blocks.title: When a breakdown step fails
rows: LPL, apoC-II, or GPIHBP1 deficiency (type I)
Fasting triglyceride often above 1,000 mg/dL (reference under 150); creamy top layer on standing
Pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, hepatosplenomegaly
ApoE2 homozygosity with a second factor (type III)
Palmar and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, premature atherosclerosis; apoE2 binds receptors poorly
blocks.caption: A block at LPL leaves whole chylomicrons in plasma; a block at apoE leaves remnants. Details of these dyslipidemias are in CV-13.

blocks.predict: Two patients have fasting plasma that is milky. In one, refrigerated plasma forms a creamy layer over a clear infranatant; in the other, the plasma stays uniformly turbid. Which fits LPL deficiency?
blocks.explain: The first. Chylomicrons are large and light enough to float to the top on standing, leaving clear plasma below because VLDL is not greatly raised. Uniform turbidity means excess VLDL, which is too small to float.

sections.title: Abetalipoproteinemia: predicting the findings of MTP deficiency

blocks.text: Abetalipoproteinemia is an autosomal recessive loss of function of MTTP, the gene for microsomal triglyceride transfer protein. Every apoB-containing lipoprotein needs MTP to be lipidated, so the defect acts in two organs at once. In the enterocyte, apoB-48 is degraded and no chylomicrons are secreted; in the hepatocyte, apoB-100 is degraded and no VLDL is secreted. Because IDL and LDL are made from VLDL, they never form either.

blocks.title: From MTP loss to the clinical picture
steps: Biallelic MTTP mutations; MTP absent
ApoB-48 and apoB-100 not lipidated and degraded
No chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, or LDL secreted
Dietary fat trapped in enterocytes; steatorrhea from infancy
Fat-soluble vitamins not delivered, vitamin E worst
Altered plasma lipids remodel red cell membranes into acanthocytes
blocks.caption: A single missing transfer protein blocks lipoprotein secretion from both intestine and liver.

blocks.text: In the gut, fat is absorbed into the enterocyte but cannot leave. Biopsy shows normal villi whose enterocytes are filled with lipid droplets, so the cells look clear or foamy, most strikingly after a fatty meal. Infants present with steatorrhea, abdominal distension, and failure to thrive. Plasma triglyceride is nearly undetectable and total cholesterol very low (often under about 50 mg/dL), apoB is absent, and triglyceride does not rise after a fat load. The liver can also become fatty, because triglyceride it makes cannot be exported as VLDL.

Vitamin E deficiency is the most severe vitamin defect because vitamin E depends on lipoproteins at both stages: it enters the blood in chylomicrons, reaches the liver in remnants, and is then loaded by alpha-tocopherol transfer protein onto VLDL for delivery to tissues. Without vitamin E, polyunsaturated membrane lipids undergo uncontrolled peroxidation. Long axons with high metabolic demand are hit first: degeneration of the dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and peripheral nerves causes loss of proprioception and vibration sense, areflexia, and ataxia, usually emerging in childhood. Photoreceptor damage, with vitamin A deficiency contributing, produces a pigmentary retinopathy resembling retinitis pigmentosa. Low vitamin K can prolong the prothrombin time, and low vitamin D can impair bone mineralization.

Acanthocytes typically make up a large fraction of red cells. Red cells exchange lipid with plasma, and in this abnormal lipid environment the outer leaflet becomes enriched in sphingomyelin relative to phosphatidylcholine. The outer leaflet expands relative to the inner one, forcing the membrane into irregular spikes. Acanthocytes do not stack into rouleaux, so the erythrocyte sedimentation rate is very low.

blocks.title: Distinguishing low and absent apoB lipoproteins from chylomicron excess
rows: No chylomicrons; VLDL and LDL present but low
Fasting triglyceride often normal; acanthocytes uncommon
Malabsorption absent; pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas
blocks.caption: Abetalipoproteinemia and LPL deficiency produce opposite plasma pictures; the MTP and SAR1B defects differ in whether the liver can still export VLDL.

blocks.title: Reasoning from a lipid panel and smear to the missing protein
blocks.text: A 10-month-old has bulky, greasy stools and poor weight gain. Fasting triglyceride is 5 mg/dL, total cholesterol 35 mg/dL, apoB undetectable, and the smear shows many spiky red cells. Step 1: steatorrhea with very low plasma triglyceride means fat is not leaving the gut, so the block is before the lymph, not at LPL (which would raise triglyceride). Step 2: absent apoB means the liver also fails to secrete VLDL, so the defect is shared by both organs, which points to MTP rather than SAR1B. Step 3: the parents' lipid levels separate recessive MTP deficiency (normal parental LDL) from homozygous hypobetalipoproteinemia (low parental LDL). Step 4: predict progressive ataxia and retinopathy from vitamin E deficiency.

sections.title: Why hepatic and intestinal lymph carry more protein than muscle lymph

blocks.text: Lymph is interstitial fluid that has entered a lymphatic capillary, so its protein concentration is set by how much plasma protein escapes the blood capillaries of the tissue it drains. Plasma total protein is about 6 to 8 g/dL, mostly albumin (about 69 kDa). How readily that protein crosses depends on endothelial structure, summarized by the reflection coefficient: near 1 when the wall holds protein back, near 0 when protein passes freely.

blocks.title: Capillary type and lymph protein
rows: Clusters of open fenestrae without diaphragms, gaps, little or no basement membrane
Tight intercellular clefts, continuous basement membrane, caveolar transcytosis
Dominated by liver and gut lymph
blocks.caption: The leakier the endothelium, the closer lymph protein comes to plasma protein (about 7 g/dL).

blocks.text: In the liver, sinusoidal endothelium has open fenestrae, intercellular gaps, and almost no basement membrane, so albumin and even larger proteins reach the space of Disse almost freely. This suits a hepatocyte that must take up protein-bound substances and secrete albumin and clotting factors directly into blood. The fluid in the space of Disse, and the hepatic lymph formed from it, therefore has nearly plasma levels of protein.

Intestinal mucosal capillaries are fenestrated. Their thin diaphragms and continuous basement membrane favor rapid exchange of water and small absorbed solutes, but they are still more permeable to protein than continuous capillaries, giving an intermediate lymph protein level. In skeletal muscle and skin, continuous capillaries let protein cross only slowly, through a small number of large pores and by vesicular transcytosis, so muscle lymph is protein poor. This low value is normal and is what sustains the oncotic gradient that limits filtration there.

Because liver and intestine produce about two thirds of all lymph, and that lymph is protein rich, they supply most of the protein carried in thoracic duct lymph. Lymph protein concentration also depends on flow: when filtration rises in a tissue with a high reflection coefficient, water outpaces protein, interstitial protein is washed out, and lymph protein falls, which is one of the safety factors against edema. Where the reflection coefficient is near zero, as in the liver, this oncotic buffer is absent, so a rise in sinusoidal pressure increases protein-rich hepatic lymph formation directly.

blocks.title: Ascites protein as a window on sinusoidal permeability
blocks.text: Two patients have ascites from raised sinusoidal pressure with a serum-ascites albumin gradient of at least 1.1 g/dL. In right heart failure, back pressure congests normal, leaky sinusoids, so filtrate keeps near-plasma protein and ascites total protein is usually 2.5 g/dL or more. In cirrhosis, collagen is laid down in the space of Disse and the endothelium loses its fenestrae (capillarization), so the wall now holds protein back like a continuous capillary; together with low serum albumin, ascites protein is usually below 2.5 g/dL.

blocks.predict: When plasma albumin falls, why does filtration rise in skin and muscle capillaries while filtration in hepatic sinusoids is barely changed by the oncotic drop?
blocks.explain: Continuous capillaries hold albumin back, so the plasma oncotic gradient opposes filtration there and lowering it increases filtration, most visibly in dependent tissues where hydrostatic pressure is highest. Hepatic sinusoids have a reflection coefficient near zero, so oncotic pressure has little influence on hepatic filtration in the first place.
blocks.check: The reflection coefficient and the paragraph on flow and safety factors.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology set the route: lacteals, mesenteric nodes, cisterna chyli, and thoracic duct deliver dietary fat to the left venous angle, so muscle, heart, and adipose tissue draw on it before the liver, which receives only the remnant. Endothelial structure, sinusoidal in the liver, fenestrated in the gut, and continuous in muscle, sets how much plasma protein each tissue's lymph returns. The same lymph that carries fat also carries lymphocytes, which is why chyle leaking from the gut wall in intestinal lymphangiectasia or from a torn thoracic duct removes fat, protein, and lymphocytes together and, if the loss persists, causes hypoalbuminemia and lymphopenia.

Biochemistry and pathology explain the defects. One gene gives two proteins through mRNA editing, one transfer protein (MTP) serves both intestine and liver, and one activator (apoC-II) and one ligand (apoE) decide where the particle unloads and where it is cleared. A missing step either prevents chylomicrons from forming (abetalipoproteinemia, with malabsorption, acanthocytes, and vitamin E neuropathy) or prevents their clearance (LPL or apoC-II deficiency, with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas). Lymph protein values are approximate, vary with species and measurement, and fall as lymph flow rises, so they describe a ranking of tissues more reliably than exact concentrations.

summary: Enterocytes rebuild absorbed 2-monoacylglycerol and fatty acids into triglyceride in the smooth ER and package it with apoB-48 into chylomicrons.
ApoB-48 comes from the same gene as apoB-100; intestinal APOBEC-1 editing creates a stop codon, removing the LDL receptor binding region.
MTP lipidates apoB as it is made; without it apoB is degraded and neither chylomicrons nor VLDL form.
Chylomicrons are too large for villus blood capillaries, enter lacteals, and reach the blood through the thoracic duct, bypassing the liver; medium chain fatty acids go directly to portal blood.
HDL donates apoC-II and apoE; apoC-II activates endothelial LPL in muscle, heart, and adipose tissue, and insulin raises adipose LPL after meals.
The cholesterol-rich remnant is cleared by the liver through apoE binding to the LDL receptor and LRP1; LPL or apoC-II deficiency leaves intact chylomicrons, and apoE2 leaves remnants.

Abetalipoproteinemia removes all apoB lipoproteins: steatorrhea with lipid-filled enterocytes, very low triglyceride and cholesterol, acanthocytes, and vitamin E deficiency with spinocerebellar ataxia and retinopathy.
Lymph protein mirrors capillary leakiness: liver (sinusoidal, about 6 g/dL) above intestine (fenestrated, about 3 to 4 g/dL) above muscle (continuous, about 2 g/dL).
Liver and gut produce most lymph and most of the protein in thoracic duct lymph; in tissues that hold protein back, rising filtration lowers lymph protein and protects against edema.

verify: Chylomicron diameter is quoted from about 75 to 1,200 nm across sources; this chapter uses roughly 100 to 1,000 nm.
Lymph protein concentrations (liver about 6 g/dL, intestine 3 to 4 g/dL, muscle and skin about 2 g/dL, thoracic duct 3 to 5 g/dL) follow Guyton and Hall; other texts give slightly different figures.
Plasma lipid values in abetalipoproteinemia (triglyceride nearly undetectable, total cholesterol often under about 50 mg/dL) vary among case series; confirm any cutoff NABNE expects.

The triglyceride level associated with type I hyperchylomicronemia and pancreatitis risk (often above 1,000 mg/dL) and the fasting reference (under 150 mg/dL) follow common consensus guidance; confirm the values NABNE uses.

The ascites total protein cutoff of 2.5 g/dL for distinguishing cardiac ascites from cirrhotic ascites, and the serum-ascites albumin gradient threshold of 1.1 g/dL, are clinical conventions; confirm whether Part I tests them.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponym Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome for abetalipoproteinemia and Anderson disease for chylomicron retention disease, or only the descriptive names.
